sentences.text: Giraffatitan was a four-legged, plant-eating sauropod dinosaur characterized by a very long neck and tail.
Specimen HMN XV2, with a fibula 13% larger than that of HMN SII, is estimated to have been 23 to 26 meters long and weighed 40 to 48 metric tons.
The brain of Giraffatitan measured approximately 300 cm3, which was small relative to its massive body size, occupying essentially the cranial vault.
Giraffatitan was once considered the largest dinosaur, but this record has been surpassed by larger titanosaurians.
Most size estimates for the species are based on the Berlin museum mount, which combines authentic bones with reconstructions.
In 1906, mining engineer Bernhard Wilhelm Sattler discovered an enormous bone at Tendaguru near Lindi in German East Africa.
The species G. brancai was named in honor of Wilhelm von Branca, who led the expedition that found the fossils in the Tendaguru Formation.
The genus Giraffatitan was established by Paul in 1988.
Evidence from tooth wear patterns suggests Giraffatitan did not have a trunk, as the wear indicates biting and tearing plants rather than grinding pre-ripped vegetation.

Historically, scientists believed the nostrils of Giraffatitan were located on the top of its head, perhaps used like a snorkel to breathe while submerged. However, studies indicate that water pressure would have prevented effective breathing underwater and that its narrow feet were unsuited for aquatic locomotion. Research by Lawrence Witmer in 2001 suggests that despite high skull openings, the nostrils were located near the snout tip, and the tall crests may have supported a fleshy resonating chamber.
A 2009 study estimated the Encephalization Quotient of Giraffatitan to be between 0.62 and 0.79, depending on the body size estimate used.

Researchers have proposed that Giraffatitan may have possessed a proboscis to aid in feeding, though this hypothesis is disputed by some colleagues who note the facial nerve was not enlarged as in elephants.
The name Giraffatitan was elevated to full genus status by George Olshevsky in 1991.

Giraffatitan fossils date to the Late Jurassic period, specifically the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian stages, placing the animal between 145 and 150 million years ago in what is now the Lindi Region of Tanzania.
While Daniel Chure rejected the separation in 2010, most studies have recognized Giraffatitan as a distinct genus since 2012.

It is debated whether the distinctive high-crested skull was a true characteristic of the genus Brachiosaurus, as the only known specimens of Brachiosaurus altithorax are now classified as Giraffatitan.
